newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai eyes Iraq for future trade.
newsitem.headline: Dubai eyes Iraq for future trade.

text.p: The Arab emirate of Dubai, the Gulf's trade and service centre, is seeking a lion's share of Iraqi business once U.N. sanctions are lifted, officials and traders said on Tuesday.
Iraq's limited oil-for-food deal with the United Nations has generated little interest in humanitarian goods available in Dubai, a trade partner before Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

But industrialists and officials say they could yet sell goods under the limited U.N. deal that lets Iraq export oil worth $1 billion every 90 days on a renewable basis. And their eyes are set on the potential Iraqi market of 20 million people when U.N. sanctions are eventually lifted.
"We are re-positioning ourselves...traditionally, the market in Dubai is capable of exporting all goods to Iraq," said Dubai Ports Authority (DPA) assistant managing director Jamal Majid bin Thaniah.

DPA runs twin ports -- Port Rashid and Jebel Ali Free Zone. The free zone, built in 1985 around what officials call the world's biggest man-made port, hosts more than 1,000 companies from 72 countries with investments of about $1.75 billion.
Iraqi traders say it offers cheaper and better goods than their neighbours Jordan and Turkey, still Iraq's main suppliers.

"Over the past year, we have made special arrangements at Jebel Ali to receive Iraq-bound goods...and send them onwards to Iraq's southern ports in smaller vessels as they cannot handle large ships there," bin Thaniah told Reuters.

"Jebel Ali is also offering facilities for Iraqi traders to open up offices quickly and practice free trade without any restrictions...they do not need a sponsor and do not pay taxes. We will also help develop Iraqi ports and their equipment."
Facilities at Iraq's Umm Qasr and Khour al-Zubair Gulf ports have not been modernised since Iraq's 1980-1988 war with Iran. Large vessels cannot reach them.
Dubai, which re-exported manufactured goods and machinery to Iraq worth 96 million dirhams ($26 million) in 1989, has made overtures toward Iraq to improve trade links.

Top port officials have visited to try to ease the flow of goods from Dubai and UAE leaders have stepped up campaigns to reconcile Gulf Arab countries that have shunned Baghdad since it invaded Kuwait.
DPA will soon open an official office in Iraq to boost cooperation, diplomats said. The UAE and Iraq have not had embassies in each other's capitals since the 1990 crisis.
Earlier this month, the UAE resumed all direct telephone, telex and telegraph links with Iraq. Iraqi businessmen say the UAE has also eased visa rules.
A 1,000 km (600 mile) highway between Amman and Baghdad is now the only route for Iraqis wishing to travel abroad and handles the bulk of Iraqi trade with the rest of the world.
